title: Dual-Band Infrared PbS Colloidal Quantum Dot Focal Plane Array

paper_content.abstract: Near-infrared and short-wave infrared dual-band detection has emerged as a pivotal enabling technology in across diverse applications spanning material identification, biological diagnostics, and machine vision. Current dual-band device architectures based on vertically stacked photodetectors such as those employing two-dimensional materials or back-illuminated colloidal quantum dots remain constrained by limited large-area manufacturability and incompatibility with standard readout integrated circuits. Here, we report a top-illuminated p-i-n-i-p dual-band photodetector using two distinct sizes of solution-processed PbS colloidal quantum dots, which enables bias-switchable spectral response between near-infrared and short-wave infrared regimes. The device achieves a specific detectivity exceeding 1×1011 cm·Hz1/2·W−1 in both bands, with short-wave infrared crosstalk of 0.5% and near-infrared crosstalk of 7.7%. The successful fabrication of a monolithic integrated 128×128 dual-band focal plane array showcases a functional dual-band infrared imager. This work establishes a scalable and silicon-compatible platform toward high-performance, low-cost dual-band infrared imagers.
paper_content.introduction:
Near-infrared (NIR, 780–1,100 nm) and short-wave infrared (SWIR, 1,100–2,500 nm) imaging technologies are garnering significant interest for applications spanning machine vision1, material identification2, and biological imaging3. Their utility in non-destructive analysis stems from the sensitivity of these spectral bands to characteristic overtone and combination vibrations of molecular bonds such as C–H, O–H, N–H, and S–H4, enabling the discrimination of materials based on their distinct chemical fingerprints. Furthermore, the differing scattering and absorption characteristics of materials in the NIR and SWIR regions result in distinct penetration depths for these two spectral bands5. This complementary behavior makes NIR/SWIR dual-band imaging a highly effectively approach for comprehensive material characterization. A representative example can be found in agricultural quality control, where the technique allows simultaneous evaluation of surface texture and internal defects—such as bruising and non-uniform ripening in apples6. As illustrated in Figure 1a, integrating dual-band imaging into optical sorting systems enhances machine vision for intelligent production, leading to more accurate and automated quality grading. By routing only premium produce to the fresh market and diverting substandard items to processed products (e.g., jam production), this technology helps minimize food waste and strengthen supply chain sustainability.

Conventional dual-band NIR/SWIR imaging systems typically employ hybrid configurations of silicon (Si)-based NIR and indium gallium arsenide (InGaAs)-based SWIR detectors, requiring complex optical alignment and post-acquisition image fusion7. Although such systems achieve useful performance, their large footprint and high cost restrict deployment in resource-constrained or portable settings. Monolithic integration of dual-band photodetectors with readout integrated circuits (ROICs) on a single substrate represents a promising alternative, enabling substantial miniaturization and system-level cost reduction. Among integrated device architectures, vertically stacked photodiodes with back-to-back junction design allow bias-selectable spectral response while maintaining high pixel utilization, an essential feature for high-resolution dual-band imaging8.

Dual-band NIR and SWIR photodetectors based on back-to-back junction architectures have been demonstrated using a variety of material systems, including inorganic thin films (e.g., Si, Ge, GeSn)9,10, two-dimensional (2D) materials (e.g., MoS , black phosphorus)11,12, and colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) (e.g., PbS, HgTe)13–15. However, Ge-based photodetectors suffer from relatively low detectivity in the SWIR range. Meanwhile, the practical deployment of 2D materials is hampered by the absence of scalable synthesis and reliable heterointegration strategies, which limits their compatibility with focal plane arrays (FPAs) manufacturing workflows9.

In contrast, CQDs, particularly those based on PbS, have emerged as a versatile material platform for both NIR and SWIR detection, owing to their bandgap tunability, solution processability, and inner compatibility with RONICs16. Pejović et al. pioneered a vertically stacked n-p-n PbS CQDs photodiode architecture that enables bias-selectable dual-band detection across the NIR and SWIR regimes14. Nevertheless, this device was implemented on a glass substrate using a back-illuminated configuration, rendering it incompatible with monolithic integration onto ROICs. Furthermore, CQDs-based dual-band photodetectors have so far been largely confined to single-pixel demonstrations, where performance is compromised by high dark current and non-negligible spectral crosstalk, there impeding their adoption in practical imaging application17.

Here, we report a top-illuminated, p-i-n-i-p structured dual-band photodetector based on two distinct sizes of PbS CQDs, enabling bias-switchable spectral response between the NIR and SWIR ranges. Through band engineering, the device achieves a specific detectivity exceeding 1×1011 cm·Hz1/2·W−1 in both bands, along with SWIR spectral crosstalk of 0.5% and NIR crosstalk of 7.7%. By monolithically integrating the CQDs photodetector array with a custom-designed ROIC featuring bidirectional current sensing, we demonstrate a 128×128 dual-band infrared FPA capable of NIR and SWIR imaging. This work establishes a scalable, Si-compatible route to high-performance dual-band infrared FPAs using solution-processed semiconductors.
paper_content.results:
Device design and working principle
We have engineered a novel dual-band photodetector employing two designed PbS CQDs absorption layers with controlled size distributions, achieving bias-selective wavelength detection. The dual-band photodetector adopts a vertically stacked p-i-n-i-p architecture comprising two back-to-back photodiodes (Figure 1b). The structure integrates a p-type PbS CQDs layer functionalized with 1,2-ethanedithiol (denoted as EDT) via solid-state ligand exchange, an intrinsic PbS CQD layer treated with halide ions via liquid-phase ligand exchange, and an n-type ZnO layer deposited by sputtering. To avoid damage to the CQDs layer, a protective fullerene (C ) layer is incorporated at the CQDs/ZnO interface. The electrical performance of the C film was evaluated via field-effect transistor measurements, as detailed in Supplementary Figure 1. The NIR photodiode, which utilizes smaller PbS CQDs (denoted as PbS-I), is positioned above the SWIR photodiode containing larger PbS CQDs (denoted as PbS-II), optimizing light absorption across both layers under top-side illumination. Optical transparency was achieved through implementation of a 100 nm indium tin oxide (ITO) top electrode, demonstrating broadband transmittance exceeding 70% across the spectral range 400–2,000 nm (Supplementary Figure 2), enabling efficient light absorption in the dual-layer structure.

Through optimized synthetic protocols, we obtained different-sized PbS CQDs with absorption peaks tailored to the NIR and SWIR spectral windows, respectively (Figure 1c). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed uniform size distributions, with mean particle diameters of 2.9 nm and 7.5 nm (Supplementary Figure 3). The batch-to-batch reproducibility of the SWIR PbS CQD synthesis was illustrated in Supplementary Figure 4. Cross-sectional TEM image of the device (Figure 1d) demonstrates that the spin-coated PbS-I and PbS-II layers exhibit good uniformity and surface smoothness. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis further confirms the presence of sharp interfacial transitions between adjacent functional layers.

The dual-band photodetector operates under a back-to-back diode configuration, as schematically depicted in Figure 1e. By reversing the bias direction across the device terminals, the NIR/SWIR photodiode can be selectively switched to a reverse-biased state, enabling spectral response to corresponding wavelength bands (Supplementary Figure 5). Additonally, the energy band alignment of the heterostructure before contact formation (Figures 1f and S6) shows a small conduction band offset (<0.4 eV), enabling efficient extraction of photogenerated electrons, while the significant valence band offset (>1.7 eV) creates a unipolar barrier that effectively blocks hole transport.

Under forward bias, the built-in electric field in the PbS-I layer sweeps out NIR-generated carriers, whereas those produced in the PbS-II layer are obstructed by the valence-band barrier (Figure 1g). Conversely, under reverse bias, SWIR photocurrent generated in the PbS-II layer is effectively collected, while NIR-generated carriers in PbS-I layer are confined (Figure 1h). By exploiting a large valence band offset as a unipolar barrier, this design not only curbs dark current by blocking majority carriers without sacrificing minority-carrier photocurrent, but also spatially confines photogenerated carriers collection to respective layers, thereby minimizing spectral crosstalk.

Dual-band performance characterization
The dark current density-voltage (J-V) characteristics (Figure 2a) exhibits typical dual-band operation, with measured dark current densities as low as 3.9 μAcm−2 at −1 V and 0.69 μAcm−2 at +1 V, indicating effective suppression of dark current. To elucidate the underlying transport mechanisms, we conducted a detailed simulation analysis of the dark current components. Under reverse bias, the dark current in the SWIR PbS diode is dominated by generation-recombination (G-R) processes. In contrast, under forward bias, trap-assisted tunneling (TAT) constitutes the dominant contribution to the dark current in the NIR PbS diode, which may be attributed to defect states introduced during ITO sputtering18, as corroborated by Supplementary Figure 7. Notably, the dark current levels attained in this dual-band photodetector are comparable to those reported for single-junction devices under reverse bias (Supplementary Table 1). To furhter evaluate the role of the barrier layer in dark current suppression, we performed a comparative analysis of devices incorporating ZnO and tetrabutylammonium iodide (TBAI)-treated PbS CQDs barrier layers (Supplementary Figure 8). The ZnO barrier layer reduces dark current by three orders of magnitude relative to the TBAI-based counterpart, identifying barrier height modulation as the principal mechanism for majority carrier confinement.

The logarithmic J-V curves under 940 nm and 1650 nm laser illumination at varying power intensities are presented in Figures 2b and 2c, while the corresponding linear J-V curves are shown in Supplementary Figure 9. The device demonstrates a pronounced photoresponse to 940 nm illumination under forward bias, while the response to 1,650 nm illumination emerges exclusively under reverse bias (Supplementary Figure 10). The dependence of photocurrent on incident light power at these wavelengths is summarized in Supplementary Figures 11 and 12. The calculated linear dynamic range (LDR) reaches 80 dB at 940 nm and 48 dB at 1,650 nm, underscoring the device’s capacity for dual-band discrimination while maintaining consistent responsivity over a broad intensity range. The calculation methods are provided in Supplementary Note 1.

To quantitatively assess the photodetection performance of the dual-band photodetector, we systematically measured both responsivity and external quantum efficiency (EQE) across the wavelength ranges of 500–1,000 nm and 1,100–2,000 nm, as shown in Figures 2d, 2e and Supplementary Figure 13. Under biases of +1 V and −1 V, the detector achieves peak responsivities of 0.13 AW−1 at 920 nm and 0.38 AW−1 at 1,765 nm, corresponding to EQE values of 17% and 26%, respectively. These results reflect efficient photon-to-electron conversion capabilities in both the NIR and SWIR regimes. Notably, a slight redshift (~30 nm) is observed between the solution absorption peak and the device EQE peak (Supplementary Figure 14). This spectral shift aligns closely with the redshift induced by ligand exchange (Supplementary Figure 15), attributed to ligand-related effects18.

To validate the reproducibility of the fabrication process, we characterized a set of 25 devices by measuring their dark currents and responsivities under ±1 V bias at 940 nm and 1,650 nm illumination (Supplementary Figure 16). The statistical analysis demonstrates good uniformity and device-to-device consistency, confirming the robustness of the fabrication methodology. Furthermore, the temporal photoresponse of the device were systematically evaluated, as shown in Supplementary Figure 17. Under 940 nm illumination, the photoresponse exhibited rise and fall times of 12.7 µs and 85.5 µs, respectively. In comparison, under 1,650 nm illumination, the device demonstrated faster response dynamics, with corrsesponding rise and fall times of 9.1 µs and 67.3 µs, respectively. These dynamic performance metric were further supported by frequency-domain measurements showing a −3 dB bandwidth of approximately 10 kHz, which closely aligns with the time-domain reponse data and demonstrates the device’s capacity for high-speed optical signals detection (Supplementary Figure 18).

Specific detectivity (D*), a critical figure of merit for evaluating photodetector performance, is defined as:

𝐷∗ = 𝑅√𝐴 / 𝑖𝑛 (1)

where R is the responsivity, i is the root mean square noise current within a 1 Hz bandwidth, and A is the device area (9.18×10−3 cm²)19. To determine 𝑖 , the current noise spectra of the dual-band device were measured at ±1 V (Figure 2f). The results show that the noise current decreases with increasing frequency, following a i ∝f −1/2 across the measured range. Importantly, at 10 kHz the noise current (0.35 pA·Hz−1/2 at −1 V and 41 fA·Hz−1/2 at +1 V) remains above the fundamental shot noise limit (96 fA·Hz−1/2 at −1 V and 20 fA·Hz−1/2 at +1 V). This behavior indicates that 1/f noise is the dominant noise source in the device within the operational frequency band. Using these values, the device achieves peak detectivities of 3.04×1011 cm·W−1·Hz1/2 for NIR and 1.04×1011 cm·W−1·Hz1/2 for SWIR, demonstrating high sensitivity across both spectral ranges.

In addition, we fabricated n-i-p-i-n structured devices (Supplementary Figure 19) and characterized their photoresponse under NIR and SWIR illumination over a range of optical power intensities (Supplementary Figure 20). While these devices retained dual-band detection functionality, both their responsivity and specitic detectivity were lower than those of the p-i-n-i-p structured counterparts. This performance difference is likely attributed to the bidirectional potential barrier in the valence band, which may hinder the efficient collection of photogenerated holes. These results underscore the critical role of precise energy band engineering in high-performance dual-band detection, as the band alignment directly governs the efficiency of carrier separation and collection in multi-junction photodetectors.

Optimization of spectral crosstalk
Spectral crosstalk represents a critical performance parameter for dual-band photodetectors, as it directly impacts their ability to accurately distinguish signals from distinct spectral bands20. In the current device architecture, the incomplete absorption of NIR light in the relatively thin PbS-I layer leads to measurable NIR-to-SWIR crosstalk under reverse bias. Although increasing the PbS-I layer thickness can enhance NIR absorption and reduce spectral crosstalk, this approach entails significant trade-offs. Owing to the inherently low carrier mobility and high density of surface trap states in CQDs films, excessive thickening PbS-I layer promotes carrier recombination during transport, thereby degrading responsivity in both the NIR and SWIR bands (Supplementary Figure 21). Given this constraint, we exploited bias-dependent spectral response as an alternative strategy to mitigate spectral crosstalk and achieve selective band detection. To quantify the effect of bias modulation, we conducted calibration experiments to establish a comprehensive responsivity matrix spanning various biases and wavelengths (Figures 3a and Supplementary Figure 22).

The responsivity matrix reveals four distinct operational regions defined by bias ranges. In Region I (0.1 V to 1 V), the device exhibits a strong response in the NIR band with minimal SWIR contribution. Region II (−0.25 V to 0.1 V) is marked by weak photoresponses across the entire spectrum. Region III (−0.25 V to −0.5 V) yields a strong response combined with a weak NIR signal, whereas Region IV (−0.5 V to −1 V) produces a broad spectral response covering both NIR and SWIR bands. In Region IV, the bottom diode (PbS-II) is reverse-biased, and the top diode (PbS-I) is forward-biased (Figure 1h). Under illumination, the resulting photocurrent is primarily contributed by electron-hole pairs generated in PbS-II due to its broadband absorption characteristics from NIR to SWIR. As the applied voltage decreases into Region III, electron-hole pairs are simultaneously generated in both diodes. However, under NIR illumination, opposing photocurrent components cancel out, preserving the SWIR selective detection (Figure 3b). Region II, the bias is insufficient to efficiently extract carriers across the inter-layer energy barriers, leading to minimal responses in both bands. Under positive voltage in Region I, only the top diode operates in reverse bias, enabling selective NIR detection (Figure 1g). Thus, spectral photoresponse can be finely tailored through external bias tuning.

To further quantify spectral crosstalk, we selected three representative operating voltages (1 V, −0.32 V, and −1 V) from regions I, III, and IV, respectively, and analyzed their normalized spectra response profiles, as shown in Figure 3c. The relative spectral crosstalk was quantified by integrating the overlap area between the NIR and SWIR response curves, normalized to the total response areas of each spectral band. The analysis yielded spectral crosstalk of 7.7% for 𝐶 and 0.5% for 𝐶 , with the detailed methodology provided in Supplementary Figure 23. These results underscore the efficacy of bias modulation in minimizing spectral crosstalk and optimizing dual-band detection performance.

Supplementary Figure 24 presents the J-V curves under 940 nm NIR illumination and dark conditions at varying optical power densities. The intersection points of the photocurrent and dark current curves define the optimum bias voltage for spectral crosstalk suppression. Remarkably, the bias voltage exhibits minimal variation (5%) across illumination intensities, demonstrating its effectiveness in suppressing spectral crosstalk over a broad range of illumination conditions. Meanwhile, the device performance was further evaluated at −0.32 V (Supplementary Figure 25), yielding a noise current density of 1.1×10−13 A·Hz1/2, and a specific detectivity of 7.6×1010 cm·Hz1/2·W−1 in the SWIR band under low incident optical power.

To systematically assess the spectral disrimination capability of the dual-band photodetector, we measured its response to 120 Hz modulated NIR and SWIR signals under controlled bias conditions, as depicted in Figures 3d and 3e. The NIR signal was generated using a xenon lamp coupled with a monochromator to produce 920 nm monochromatic light, while the SWIR signal was derived from an 800°C blackbody source filtered through a long-pass filter with a 1 µm cutoff wavelength. At +1 V, the device exhibited strong responsivity to the NIR signal but negligible response to the SWIR signal. Conversely, at −0.32 V, the device showed pronounced SWIR detection while effectively suppressing the NIR signal. At −1 V, the device demonstrated broadband responsivity, enabling simultaneous detection of both spectra bands. These results confirm that bias voltage modulation effectively minimizes spectral crosstalk between NIR and SWIR signals. In addition, the feasibility of sequential NIR and SWIR signals readout was demonstrated, as illustrated in Supplementary Figures 26 and 27.

Subsequently, the device was subjected to extended cycling tests under 940 nm and 1650 nm illumination to evaluate its reliability in dual-band detection. As shown in Supplementary Figure 28, both photocurrent and dark current remained stable over 1,000 continuous cycles. To rigorously assess the operational stability, we further subjected the device to a continuous bias stress test under constant illumination. As presented in Supplementary Figure 29, the device exhibited negligible degradation in photocurrent over a 10,000 s period under both +1 V (NIR mode) and -1 V (SWIR mode) biases, confirming robust operation under realistic working conditions. We further characterized the shelf-life stability of PbS CQDs films and devices by monitoring their optical and electrical properties under different storage conditions. As shown in Supplementary Figure 30, the absorption spectra of ligand-exchanged films exhibit negligible shifts after 20 days in both air and nitrogen (N2), indicating robust optical stability. Electrically, the field-effect transistors based on PbS CQDs fabricated on Si/SiO2 substrates with Ti/Au electrodes retained nearly identical transfer characteristics after 20 days of N2 storage (Supplementary Figure 31a), confirming excellent electrical stability in inert environments. In contrast, devices stored in ambient air exhibited a gradual decline in conductivity and carrier mobility, dropping to 50% and 40% of initial values after 20 days, respectively (Supplementary Figure 31b). This degradation is attributed to co-oxidation by atmospheric O2 and moisture, leading to the formation of insulating PbSO3 or PbSO4 species at dot surfaces or interfaces21, which increases charge hopping barriers and impair transport performance. Consistent with these findings, device-level performance showed mild degradation after two weeks in air, with slight reductions in both dark and photocurrents in the NIR and SWIR bands (Supplementary Figure 32a). Crucially, devices stored in a N2-purged environment for 15 months retain nearly all initial performance, with no significant change in dark current or responsivity (Supplementary Figure 32b). These results affirm the intrinsic stability of the material system when isolated from the ambient atmosphere. However, achieving practical long-term reliability requires further comprehensive studies, particularly regarding the development and assessment of effective encapsulation strategies.

A comprehensive benchmarking analysis against state-of-the-art dual-band photodetectors reported9–13,17,20,22–24 is systematically summarized in Supplementary Table 2 and Figure 3f. Our device achieves a room-temperature D* exceeding 1×1011 cm·Hz1/2·W−1 in both NIR and SWIR bands, with spectral crosstalk below 1%, outperforming most existing dual-band photodetectors. These combined characteristics enable high-fidelity dual-band infrared imaging, positioning the device as a promising solution candidate for multispectral sensing applications.

Dual-band infrared imaging
A custom ROIC was designed to operate under both positive and negative bias conditions, with its schematic diagram illustrated in Supplementary Figure 33. Under reverse bias, the photodetector generates a cathodic photocurrent that is injected into the capacitive trans-impedance amplifier (CTIA) input node, leading to a linear decrease in output voltage during integration. Conversely, under forward bias, the anodic photocurrent flows out of the CTIA input, resulting in a rising output voltage. By carefully tuning the DC bias levels of the reference voltage and the internal operational amplifiers, the output swing range is symmetrically configured to accommodate both polarities of photocurrent integration. The fabrication process of the dual-band FPA is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 34. The resulting dual-band FPA features an array size of 128×128 with a 15 μm pixel pitch, as shown in Figure 4a. The dual-band imaging system, depicted in Figure 4b, utilizes a lens to focus tungsten light reflected from the target onto the dual-band FPA. The ROIC controls the bias voltage of the FPA, while a dedicated circuit board collects and processes the signals, enabling image reconstruction through custom software. The system achieves a frame rate of 333 Hz with a 2 ms integration time and 1 ms readout time. The complete experimental setup is presented in Supplementary Figure 35.

As shown in Supplementary Figures 36 and 37, the dual-band FPA exhibits effective pixel rates of 87.99% and 90.76% functional elements in NIR and SWIR bands, respectively. This non-uniformity primarily arises from surface unevenness of the ROIC (Supplementary Figure 38), which introduces variations in pixel response. In comparison, the PbS CQDs film spin-coated on the flat substrate exhibit a markedly lower roughness of only 3 nm (Supplementary Figure 39). Adopting planarization processes in future ROIC is expected to reduce defective pixel rates and improve spatial uniformity. Furthermore, the image data processing workflow is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 40.

To demonstrate the dual-band imaging capability, we constructed a test scene comprising the Fudan university emblem printed on a white paper, partially overlaid with acrylic paint and a Si wafer. Figure 4c compares images captured using a standard complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor (CIS) with those capatured by the dual-band FPA operating in NIR and SWIR modes. In the NIR mode, the dual-band FPA clearly resolved the emblem pattern beneath the acrylic paint, leveraging the strong NIR transmission through organic materials. Conversely, in the SWIR mode, the FPA successfully imaged the emblem pattern obscured by the Si wafer, ultilizing the characteristic of SWIR light to transmit through Si. These results highlight the complementary nature of NIR and SWIR imaging modalities, achieving precise target identification in complex, layered scenarios through spectral discrimination. As shown in Figure 4d, different colored inks exhibit distinct absorption behaviors across the NIR and SWIR bands. Red ink remains undetectable in both NIR and SWIR images, whereas green ink is clearly visible under NIR illumination but becomes faint in the SWIR. In contrast, black ink is discernible in both spectral bands. These marked differences in spectral response enable the design of effective anti-counterfeiting markers. Figure 4e further illustrates the differential absorption properties of water, acetone, polyethylene (PE), and ink in the NIR and SWIR regions. When contained in white PE bottles, water and acetone are not observable under visible light. The NIR image reveals the meniscus of water but not that of acetone, whereas both menisci are clearly observed in the SWIR image, with water appearing darker due to stronger absorption. The ink markings on the bottle surface are prominent in the NIR image but fade in the SWIR image. Additionally, Supplementary Figure 41 shows imaging results of the NIR/SWIR dual-band FPA in other scenarios. Collectively, these results confirm that the distinct NIR and SWIR absorption can be effectively utilized for spectral identification.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of PbS colloidal quantum dots
NIR-absorbing PbS CQDs were synthesized using a hot-injection approach. A mixture of PbO (0.45 g), oleic acid (OA, 1.5 mL), and octadecene (ODE, 22.5 mL) was degassed under vacuum (10−3 mbar) at 100°C for 1 hour until a clear solution formed. Under N2 atmosphere, bis(trimethylsilyl) sulfide (TMS2S, 180 µL in 3 mL octadecene) was swiftly injected, leading to rapid nucleation and a color change to dark brown. The resulting PbS CQDs were purified with hexane and acetone, then redispersed in octane at a concentration of 50 mg·mL−1.

SWIR-absorbing PbS CQDs were synthesized using a two-step hot-injection process. Lead oleate was first formed by dissolving PbO (0.446 g) in a mixture of ODE (22.5 mL) and OA (2.5 mL) under N2 at 130°C for 1 hour. The first sulfur precursor (53 µL TMS2S in 3 mL ODE) was injected and reacted for 20 minutes, followed by injection of the second sulfur precursor (30 µL TMS2S in 3 mL ODE) and further reaction for 15 minutes. The resulting PbS CQDs were purified with hexane and acetone, then redispersed in octane at a concentration of 50 mg·mL−1.

Ligand exchange
The solution-phase ligand-exchange process was conducted in a N2-filled glovebox. For NIR-absorbing PbS CQDs, a ligand solution containing PbI2 (0.01 M), PbBr2 (0.04 M), and ammonium acetate (0.06 M) in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). An octane solution of OA-capped PbS CQDs (20 mg·mL−1) was added, and the mixture was vigorously shaken for 5 minutes to introduce phase transfer into DMF. After three washes with hexane, the PbS CQDs were precipitated with toluene, isolated by centrifugation, vacuum-dried for 20 minutes, and redispersed in a butylamine (TBA)/DMF mixture (1:1 by volume) at 400 mg·mL−1.

For SWIR-absorbing PbS CQDs, a mixed halide-based ligand solution was prepared by dissolving PbI2 (0.05 M), PbBr2 (0.04 M), PbCl2 (0.05 M), and sodium acetate (0.044 M) in DMF. A PbS CQDs solution (~6 mg·mL−1 in octane) was added, and the mixture was vigorously shaken to transfer the CQDs into the DMF phase. After removing octane, the solution was washed three times with octane. The PbS CQDs were then precipitated by adding toluene, centrifuged, vacuum-dried for 20 minutes, and redispersed in a DMF/TBA mixture (1:1 by volume) at 300 mg·mL-1.

Device fabrication
The dual-band PbS CQDs photodetectors were fabricated on Si/SiO2 substrates pre-patterned with 5 nm Ti/10 nm Au bottom contacts. A 50 nm PbS-EDT layer was first deposited via a layer-by-layer method. The OA-capped PbS-CQDs were spin-coated at 2,000 r.p.m. for 40 s, treated with a 0.01% volume ratio of EDT in acetonitrile for 20 s and then washed by acetonitrile, and this process was repeated twice. Subsequently, the SWIR-absorbing layer (PbS-II, ~110 nm) was spin-coated at 4,000 r.p.m. for 60 s from a 300 mg·mL−1 CQDs inks. Next, a 50 nm C60 layer was thermally evaporated, followed by the deposition of a 50 nm ZnO layer via magnetron sputtering, serving as the electron transport layers. Furthermore, the NIR-absorbing layer (PbS-I, ~140 nm) was then spin-coated at 4,000 r.p.m. for 60 s using 400 mg·mL−1 CQDs ink and capped with two additional PbS-EDT layers. Finally, a transparent ITO top electrode was deposited by magnetron sputtering at room temperature.

Dual-band FPA fabrication
The ROIC for the dual-band FPA was fabricated in a 0.18 μm CMOS process. After cleaning the chip, a Ti/Au (150/50 nm) bottom electrode was patterned by UV lithography and electron beam evaporation, expanding the pixel size to 12×12 μm. Two PbS-EDT layers were deposited via spin-coated and solid-state ligand exchange. Subsequently, SWIR-absorbing PbS CQDs (PbS-II) were spin-coated from solution using a liquid-phase ligand exchange process and annealed at 85°C for 15 minutes. Then, a 50 nm C60 layer was thermally evaporated, followed by a 50 nm ZnO layer deposited as electron transport layers by magnetron sputtering. NIR-absorbing PbS CQDs (PbS-I) were spin-coated, annealed under the same conditions, and covered with two additional PbS-EDT layers via solid-state ligand exchange as hole transport layers. Finally, a 100 nm ITO top electrode was sputtered to complete the device structure. The completed dual-band FPA was wire-bonded to a testing circuit board for performance evaluation.

Material characterization
Optical absorption spectra were recorded using a Hitachi U-4100 Plus spectrophotometer. Cross-sectional TEM samples of PbS CQDs dual-band photodetectors were prepared using the focused ion beam lift-out technique on a Tescan GAIA3 system. TEM imaging and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping were collected using a Thermo Fisher TALOS F200X system. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) was performed under ultrahigh vacuum (~10−10 mbar) using a KRATOS AXIS Ultra DLD system with a monochromatic HeI (21.22 eV) excitation source.

Device characterization
The J-V curves and time-dependent photocurrent under dark conditions and 940 nm illumination were performed using an MS200 system equipped with a Keithley 6482 semiconductor analyzer. The transient response and −3 dB bandwidth were recorded using the same setup together with a PicoScope 4262 oscilloscope and an SR570 low-noise current preamplifier (Stanford Research Systems). Noise currents of the PbS CQDs photodiode were measured using a semiconductor parameter analyzer (FS-Pro, Primarius Technologies). The EQE spectral at each wavelength was determined using a lock-in amplifier (Stanford Research Systems, SR865A), a chopper, an SR570 low-noise current preamplifier, and a Horiba iHR350 spectrometer equipped with a xenon lamp and a tungsten lamp.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a highly significant and innovative work on the development of a monolithically integrated, dual-band (NIR/SWIR) infrared focal plane array (FPA) using solution-processed PbS colloidal quantum dots (CQDs). The novel p-i-n-i-p unipolar barrier heterostructure design, achieving bias-switchable spectral discrimination with exceptionally low crosstalk and high detectivity, represents a major advancement in low-cost, high-performance multispectral infrared imaging. The successful demonstration of a functional 128×128 FPA prototype with real-world imaging applications underscores the technological impact of this work. The manuscript is well-written, logically structured, and supported by comprehensive data. It is suitable for publication after addressing the points below.
1.While operability is mentioned (Fig. S23), quantitative data on pixel-to-pixel uniformity (e.g., histogram of responsivity or dark current across the array) for both bands should be provided, which would strengthen the assessment of FPA manufacturability.
2.The ROIC readout speed (frame rate) for the demonstrated FPA is not stated. Providing this would help contextualize its suitability for real-time applications.
3.Page 6 mentions the PbS-I layer thickness limits NIR absorption, contributing to residual crosstalk. Was thickness optimization performed? Could a slight increase further reduce NIR→SWIR crosstalk without compromising SWIR response or speed?
4.The ligand exchange process is critical for performance. Briefly commenting on the reproducibility and stability of the exchanged films (e.g., shelf-life, environmental stability) would be beneficial.
5.The energy band diagrams (Fig. 1f, S4) are schematic. Adding estimated values (e.g., from UPS/IPES or simulation) for the conduction/valence band offsets and Fermi level positions would provide deeper insight into the carrier blocking/extraction mechanisms.
6.How do the reported detectivity and dark current values for each band in the dual-band device compare to state-of-the-art single-band PbS CQD detectors? This would highlight the efficiency of the integrated design.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Submitted paper entitled “Dual-Band Infrared PbS Colloidal Quantum Dot Focal Plane Array” presents a dual-band infrared imaging system based on a vertically stacked configuration of oppositely oriented near-infrared (NIR) and short-wave infrared (SWIR) absorbing PbS CQD layers. The authors report dark current densities on the order of 10⁻⁶ A and EQE of ~25%, followed by dual-wavelength imaging demonstrations. While the experimental realization is technically competent, the manuscript, in its current form, falls short of the scientific depth expected for a publication in Nature Communications. The work reads more as a mid-level engineering report/demonstration than a contribution of fundamental scientific insight. I recommend either submitting this manuscript to a more engineering- or imaging-focused journal, or doing more experimental designs and substantially revising it to clearly articulate and support a meaningful scientific question or hypothesis. Below, I outline several concerns and suggestions:
1. The use of PbS CQDs for infrared detection and imaging has been extensively explored and commercialized. The device architecture, including the hole/electron transport layers and charge blocking strategies, appears to rely on well-established approaches that have been in the literature for over a decade.
2. While PbS CQDs are widely considered the gold standard among CQD materials, their intrinsic ionic character leads to well-known issues with operational and environmental instability. The device architecture employed here has previously been shown to suffer from performance degradation under electrical bias and prolonged operation. However, the manuscript does not address these stability concerns, either through experimental investigation or discussion.
3. The authors state that the concept of dual-band CQD-based imaging has been previously demonstrated across several architectures. It is unclear what the central innovation of this work is. If the novelty lies in the monolithic integration on a focal plane array (FPA), this aspect is confined to a brief discussion centered around Figure 4 and does not sufficiently elevate the scientific significance.
4. The manuscript does not clearly articulate the scientific challenge being addressed or the fundamental insight offered by this study. As a result, the broader implications for the CQD or imaging community remain unclear.
5. The proposed architecture may face limitations for real-world imaging applications. Notably, the system appears to require relatively high bias voltages to achieve meaningful contrast, which can negatively affect device stability, induce ghost imaging artifacts, and slow response times.
6. Due to the opposing orientation of the stacked junctions, the internal electric fields generated upon illumination in each spectral band are in opposite directions. This raises the possibility of electrostatic coupling or cancellation effects, whereby excitation in one junction perturbs the band alignment and detection fidelity in the other. This undermines the assumption of independent dual-band detection and should be thoroughly investigated.
7. Several figures contain data that appear inconsistent. The authors are encouraged to carefully review their measurements, ensure statistical significance, and include reproducibility assessments.
8. The images presented in Figure 4 are difficult to interpret. Aside from panel c, the differences among the panels are subtle or unclear.
9. The experimental section lacks sufficient detail on the fabrication of both the devices and the integrated FPA. More comprehensive information is needed to ensure reproducibility and to assess the scalability or practicality of the proposed approach.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Below are our point-to-point responses to the reviewers’ comments. We have uploaded our manuscript with the revised parts marked red in the main text and Supporting Information file.
Reviewer #1:
This manuscript presents a highly significant and innovative work on the development of a monolithically integrated, dual-band (NIR/SWIR) infrared focal plane array (FPA) using solution-processed PbS colloidal quantum dots (CQDs). The novel p-i-n-i-p unipolar barrier heterostructure design, achieving bias-switchable spectral discrimination with exceptionally low crosstalk and high detectivity, represents a major advancement in low-cost, high-performance multispectral infrared imaging. The successful demonstration of a functional 128×128 FPA prototype with real-world imaging applications underscores the technological impact of this work. The manuscript is well-written, logically structured, and supported by comprehensive data. It is suitable for publication after addressing the points below.
We appreciate the favorable and helpful comments on our work.
Comment 1-1. While operability is mentioned (Fig. S23), quantitative data on pixel-to-pixel uniformity (e.g., histogram of responsivity or dark current across the array) for both bands should be provided, which would strengthen the assessment of FPA manufacturability.
Response 1-1: Thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion.
To quantitatively assess pixel-to-pixel uniformity and manufacturability of the FPA, we have performed a statistical analysis of the dark and photocurrent (converted to voltage via the readout circuit) across the entire array in both NIR and SWIR modes, as shown in the updated Figure S33.
The results demonstrate good uniformity across the array. Specifically, in the NIR mode, the dark signal shows an average voltage of –9.0 mV (σ = 20.4 mV), while the photoresponse under illumination averaged –136.4 mV (σ = 20.4 mV). In the SWIR mode, the average dark voltage was 47.2 mV (σ = 44.1 mV), and the average photoresponse reached 188 mV (σ = 84.4 mV).
In the main text on page 15, we added:
“As shown in Figure S32 and S33, the dual-band FPA exhibits effective pixel rates of 87.99% and 90.76% functional elements in NIR and SWIR bands, respectively.”
Meanwhile, we added the Figure S33 and the corresponding description in the Supporting Information on page S24 and page S25:
“Figure S33. Statistical distribution of the dark noise voltage and the signal voltage under uniform tungsten lamp illumination for the dual-band FPA in the NIR and SWIR operating modes.
“The performance of the FPA was characterized by analyzing dark-current and flat-field response images in both the NIR and SWIR spectral bands to quantify the defective pixel ratio. Pixels with responses exceeding twice the mean response value are defined as overheated pixels, while those below half the mean response value are classified as dead pixels11. Based on analysis of dark and uniform illumination images, the defective pixel rates for NIR and SWIR modes were calculated to be 12.01% and 9.24%, respectively. Furthermore, the dark signal in the NIR mode averaged -9.0 mV (σ = 20.4 mV), while the photoresponse under illumination averaged -136.4 mV (σ = 78.7 mV). Corresponding values for the SWIR mode were 47.2 mV (σ = 44.1 mV) for the dark signal and 188 mV (σ = 84.4 mV) for the photoresponse.”
Reference:
11. Mu, G. et al. Visible to mid-wave infrared PbS/HgTe colloidal quantum dot imagers. Nat. Photonics 18, 1147–1154 (2024).
Comment 1-2. The ROIC readout speed (frame rate) for the demonstrated FPA is not stated. Providing this would help contextualize its suitability for real-time applications.
Response 1-2: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
The demonstrated FPA achieves a frame rate of 333 Hz, corresponding to an integration time of 2 ms and a readout time of 1ms.
In the main text on page 15, we added:
“The system achieves a frame rate of 333 Hz with a 2 ms integration time and 1 ms readout time.”
Comment 1-3. Page 6 mentions the PbS-I layer thickness limits NIR absorption, contributing to residual crosstalk. Was thickness optimization performed? Could a slight increase further reduce NIR→SWIR crosstalk without compromising SWIR response or speed?
Response1-3: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
We have systematically investigated the effect of PbS-I (NIR absorption layer) thickness on device performance. As suggested, increasing the thickness of the PbS-I layer does indeed help reduce NIR→SWIR spectral crosstalk due to enhanced NIR absorption. However, we observed a concomitant decrease in SWIR responsivity. This trade-off is likely attributed to increased carrier recombination losses for SWIR-generated photocurrent as the carriers travel a longer path through the thicker layer.
In the main text on page 10 and page 11, we added:
“Although increasing the PbS-I layer thickness can enhance NIR absorption and reduce spectral crosstalk, this approach entails significant trade-offs. Owing to the inherently low carrier mobility and high density of surface trap states in CQDs films, excessive thickening PbS-I layer promotes carrier recombination during transport, thereby degrading responsivity in both the NIR and SWIR bands, (Figure S18). Given this constraint, we exploited bias-dependent spectral response as an alternative strategy to mitigate spectral crosstalk and achieve selective band detection.”
Meanwhile, we added the Figure S18 in the Supporting Information on page S13.
“Figure S18. Dependence of responsivity at 940 nm and 1650 nm, and spectral crosstalk, on the thickness of the PbS-I film in the dual-band device.”
Comment 1-4: The ligand exchange process is critical for performance. Briefly commenting on the reproducibility and stability of the exchanged films (e.g., shelf-life, environmental stability) would be beneficial.
Response 1-4: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
To evaluate reproducibility, we fabricated three independent batches of PbS CQD films using the solution-phase ligand exchange process. As shown in Figure 1, the absorption peaks of these films exhibit a variation of less than 10 nm, indicating good batch-to-batch consistency and minimal aggregation during the ligand exchange process.
Figure 1. Absorption spectra of films after ligand exchange performed in three different batches.
Regarding environmental stability, we investigated both optical and electrical properties under different storage conditions. As presented in Figure S26, the absorption spectra of the ligand-exchanged films show negligible spectral shift after 20 days of storage in both air and nitrogen atmospheres, demonstrating good optical stability.
For electrical stability, we fabricated field-effect transistors with Ti/Au electrodes on Si/SiO substrates to monitor the transfer characteristics and conductivity of the PbS CQD films. As shown in Figure S27a, the transfer curves remain nearly unchanged after 20 days of storage in N , confirming excellent electrical stability under inert conditions. However, as illustrated in Figure S27b, the conductivity and carrier mobility of films stored in ambient air gradually decrease over time. After 20 days, the conductivity drops to 50% and the mobility to 40% of their initial values. This degradation is likely caused by co-oxidation from atmospheric oxygen and moisture, leading to the formation of insulating PbSO andPbSO species at the quantum dot surfaces or interfaces[1]. This increases the energy barrier for carrier hopping and reduces charge transport efficiency.
In summary, the ligand exchange process is reproducible, and the resulting films exhibit robust optical stability. However, long-term preservation of optimal electrical performance requires storage in an inert atmosphere. We have added this discussion along with the relevant data in the revised manuscript and Supplementary Information, to better address the stability aspect.
Reference:
[1] Tang, J. et al. Quantum dot photovoltaics in the extreme quantum confinement regime: The surface-chemical origins of exceptional air- and light-stability. ACS Nano 4, 869–878 (2010).
In the main text on page 13, we added:
“We further characterized the environmental stability of PbS CQDs films and devices by monitoring their optical and electrical properties under different storage conditions. As shown in Figure S26, the absorption spectra of ligand-exchanged films exhibit negligible shifts after 20 days in both air and nitrogen (N ), indicating robutst optical stability. Electrically, the field-effect transistors based on PbS CQDs fabricated on Si/SiO substrates with Ti/Au electrodes retained nearly identical transfer characteristics after 20 days of N storage (Figure S27a), confirming excellent electrical stability in inert environments. In contrast, devices stored in ambient air exhibited a gradual decline in conductivity and carrier mobility, dropping to 50% and 40% of initial values after 20 days, respectively (Figure S27b). This degradation is attributed to co-oxidation by atmospheric O and moisture, leading to the formation of insulating PbSO or PbSO species at dot surfaces or interfaces21, which increases charge hopping barriers and impair transport performance.”

Response 1-5: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
We have performed UPS and UV-Vis absorption measurements to experimentally determine the valence band maximum, conduction band minimum, and Fermi level positions of the key materials: PbS-II, ZnO, and C . These results are now included in 60 Figure S4 of the revised Supporting Information. The band energy levels of PbS-I and EDT were referenced from our previous report[1].

In the main text on page 6, we added:
“Additionally, the energy band alignment of the heterostructure before contact formation (Figures 1f and S4) shows a small conduction band offset (<0.4 eV), enabling efficient extraction of photogenerated electrons, while the significant valence band offset (>1.7 eV) creates a unipolar barrier that effectively blocks hole transport.”

To elucidate the energy landscape governing charge transport, we systematically characterized the band alignment architecture of the multilayer device through complementary spectroscopic analyses. The Fermi levels positions and valence band maxima were UPS directly measured by UPS. Comment 1-6: How do the reported detectivity and dark current values for each band in the dual-band device compare to state-of-the-art single-band PbS CQD detectors? This would highlight the efficiency of the integrated design.
Response 1-6: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
To provide a comprehensive assessment, we have summarized the performance metrics of PbS photodiodes in Table S1.
Single-band PbS CQD photodiodes typically operate near 0 V bias, resulting in detectivity values that can exceed 1×1012 cm·Hz1/2·W−1. In contrast, our dual-band device requires an applied bias to enable efficient charge separation and collection across both NIR and SWIR spectral channels. Consequently, the detectivity of our dual-band device is relatively lower compared to these optimal single-band detectors due to the inherent increase in dark current at non-zero biases.
However, it is important to note that the dark current levels at operating bias in our dual-band device are comparable to those reported for state-of-the-art single-band PbS CQD detectors. This indicates that our integrated design maintains competitive noise performance, which is crucial for practical dual-band imaging applications.

Comment 1-7: The 1000-cycle test (Fig. S19) shows excellent short-term stability. Commenting on potential degradation mechanisms (e.g., oxidation, ion migration) and any preliminary data on longer-term stability under ambient or operational conditions would be useful for assessing practical viability.
Response 1-7: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
To evaluate environmental stability, we monitored device performance after storage in ambient air for two weeks. As shown in Figure S28a, the dark current and photocurrent in both the NIR and SWIR bands exhibit a slight degradation. This mild performance decline is likely attributed to oxidation-induced reduction in charge carrier mobility within the quantum dot film, possibly due to the formation of surface oxides or trap states that hinder carrier transport. Interestingly, the device-level degradation is significantly slower than that observed in bare quantum dot films, which we attribute to the partial environmental protection provided by the top-layer ITO electrode.
As shown in Figure S28b, the devices stored in a nitrogen-purged environment for 15 months retained nearly all of its initial performance, with no significant change in dark current or responsivity, confirming the intrinsic stability of the materials when shielded from ambient atmosphere.
These results suggest that the primary degradation mechanisms—likely involving oxygen and moisture-induced oxidation and possibly ion migration—are effectively mitigated by proper encapsulation. Therefore, for practical applications, we recommend hermetic packaging using metal or ceramic housings with inert gas sealing to ensure long-term reliability of the quantum dot image sensors.

Response 1-8: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
The circuit, as shown in Figure S29, enables dual-band detection by supporting the integration of bidirectional photocurrents. Under reverse bias, the photodetector generates a cathodic photocurrent that is injected into the CTIA input node, causing the output voltage to decrease linearly during integration. Conversely, under forward bias, the anodic photocurrent flows out of the CTIA input, resulting in a rising output voltage. By carefully tuning the DC bias levels of the reference voltage (V ) and the operational ref amplifiers within the CTIA, the output swing range is symmetrically optimized for both upward and downward integration. This dual-mode operation is essential for independent readout of NIR and SWIR signals in our dual-band detector.
We have added this explanation to the caption and discussion of Figure S29 in the Supplementary Information to provide clearer insight into the circuit’s key features.
In the main text on page 15, we added:
“Under reverse bias, the photodetector generates a cathodic photocurrent that is injected into the capacitive trans-impedance amplifier (CTIA) input node, leading to a linear decrease in output voltage during integration. Conversely, under forward bias, the anodic photocurrent flows out of the CTIA input, resulting in a rising output voltage. By carefully tuning the DC bias levels of the reference voltage and the internal operational amplifiers, the output swing range is symmetrically configured to accommodate both polarities of photocurrent integration.”
Meanwhile, the related context was added in the Supporting Information on page S20 and page S21:
“Figure S29. Detailed pixel circuit diagram.
The photocurrent from the PbS CQD photodetector is integrated using a CTIA architecture, selected for its high injection efficiency and input linearity10. The CTIA converts the photocurrent into a voltage signal and accumulates charge onto the integration capacitor, stabilizing the input node voltage and thereby minimizing dark current fluctuation. Additionally, the circuit supports both forward and reverse bias operation by maintaining a constant reference voltage (V ) while adjusting the bias at the photodetector cathode.

However, these previous dual-band devices were typically built on ITO glass with bottom illumination through the substrate, which is fundamentally incompatible with monolithic integration onto silicon-based ROICs. This back-illuminated architecture prevents direct pixel-to-pixel coupling with ROICs and has thus limited dual-band CQD imaging to single-pixel or scanning-based systems.
The key innovation of our work lies in the first design and realization of a top-illuminated dual-band CQD photodetector based on a vertically stacked architecture. By engineering the device stack for top-side illumination, we enable direct integration with ROICs in a FPA configuration. Moreover, we optimized the device structure to achieve high detectivity, low spectral crosstalk and developed a bidirectional readout circuit to independently address the NIR and SWIR channels.
This work represents the first demonstration of NIR/SWIR dual-band imaging using a CQD FPA. This advancement provides a scalable and practical pathway toward low-cost, high-performance multispectral imaging systems based on solution-processed quantum dots.

Comment 2-6:The uniformity is not very good compared to reported CQD broadband PD or dual band bulk material PD. Is it come from the uniform doping? What is the roughness of each material layer? How to solve this problem?
Response 2-6: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
Our analysis attributes the primary source of non-uniformity to the inherent topographical variations of the ROIC surface. As evidenced by Figure S34, the fabricated ROIC exhibits micrometer-scale height variations across the pixel array. The solution-processed PbS CQD film, with the thickness of less than 500 nm, is highly susceptible to such substrate topography during spin-coating. This conformity to the underlying surface directly leads to pixel-to-pixel variations in film thickness, morphology, and consequently, photoresponse.
To isolate the influence of substrate topography, we fabricated control devices on flat Si/SiO substrates. Atomic force microscope (AFM) characterization of these control 2 devices reveals a substantially lower surface roughness of only 3.0 nm RMS (Figure S35). The significantly improved uniformity achieved on these flat substrates provide compelling evidence that substrate planarity is a critical factor for the performance homogeneity of solution-processed CQD FPAs.
To address the fundamental issue in future iterations, we propose a co-design and optimization framework between the ROIC and the photodetector stack. From a fabrication perspective, this will involve the introduction of an additional chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) step within the back-end-of-line process of the ROIC. This targeted planarization protocol is designed to achieve sub-5 nm RMS surface topography prior to CQD deposition, thereby ensuring a uniform substrate for subsequent solution-processing[1].
Reference:
[1] Klem, E. J. D., Gregory, C. W., Temple, D. S. & Lewis, J. S. Colloidal quantum dot 29 vis-SWIR imaging: Demonstration of a focal plane array and camera prototype (presentation recording). in Optical Sensing, Imaging, and Photon Counting: Nanostructured Devices and Applications vol. 9555 28–28 (SPIE, 2015).

Comment 2-7: Figure 1c and Figure 2e. The cut off wavelength of absorption and photoresponse spectra of SWIR do not agree with each other. Explain it.
Response 2-7: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
The observed discrepancy in the cutoff wavelength between the absorption spectrum (Figure 1c) and the photoresponse spectrum (Figure 2e) arises primarily from the intrinsic batch-to-batch variation inherent in our quantum dot synthesis. These characterizations were performed on samples fabricated from two different CQD batches. To quantitatively assess this variation, we synthesized and characterized nine independent batches of SWIR PbS CQDs under nominally identical conditions. The absorption peak positions, as summarized in Figure S12, follow a distribution centered at 1650 nm with a standard deviation of 96.3 nm. The spectral difference between the devices in Figure 1c and 2e falls well within this statistical distribution. We attributed this batch-to-batch variation to the two-injection synthesis protocol, where minor fluctuations in critical parameters—such as the injection or timing of sulfur precursor—are known to exert a significant impact on the final quantum dot size.
Therefore, the observed offset between the absorption and photoresponse cutoff wavelengths is mainly due to synthesis batch variability, rather than measurement error or fundamental device physics. We have added a discussion of this point in the revised manuscript, to clarify the origin of the spectral shift.
Reference:
[1] Kirmani, A. R., Walters, G., Kim, T., Sargent, E. H. & Amassian, A. Optimizing solid-state ligand exchange for colloidal quantum dot optoelectronics: How much is enough? ACS Appl. Energy Mater. 3, 5385–5392 (2020).

Response 3-14: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
Regarding Figure 3a, we have expanded our discussion to better explain it. Specifically, in region IV, the bottom diode (PbS-II) is reverse biased, whereas the top diode (PbS-I) is forward biased (Figure 1g). Consequently, when exposed to light, the output photocurrent is primarily contributed by electron-hole pairs generated in PbS-II due to its broadband absorption characteristics from NIR to SWIR. As the applied voltage decreases into region III, electron-hole pairs are simultaneously generated in both diodes, but under NIR illumination, these pairs tend to cancel out, preserving the SWIR response. Further lowering the bias into region II results in insufficient energy for carriers to overcome barriers between absorption and transport layers, leading to weak responses in both bands. When applying positive voltage in region I, only the top diode operates in reverse bias, focusing the response solely on the NIR band. Thus, wavelength-dependent photoresponse can be finely tuned by adjusting the external bias.

Comment 4-1: The use of PbS CQDs for infrared detection and imaging has been extensively explored and commercialized. Response 4-1: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the maturity of PbS CQDs technology. The true novelty of this work, however, lies not in the individual layer constituents, but in the first dual-band photodetector stack engineered for top-side illumination and direct FPA integration.
While employing established single-band concepts, we tackled unique challenges in spectral crosstalk suppression—issues inherent to our dual-band architecture but absent in single-junction devices. Our key innovations form a cohesive development pipeline: first, we re-engineered the device stack to facilitate top-side illumination while maintaining high-detectivity–a configuration that is critical for direct coupling with 50 ROICs in an FPA. Building upon this foundation, we developed a tailored optimization protocol to achieve the essential low spectral crosstalk between NIR and SWIR. Finally, we conceived a novel bidirectional readout circuit to independently access the two photodiodes, thereby enabling NIR/SWIR dual-band data acquisition.
This work thereby provides the first experimental demonstration of a solution-processed, dual-band CQD-FPA capable of simultaneous NIR/SWIR imaging. We have revised the manuscript to more explicitly frame our work within this context of integration science, clarifying that its primary contribution is a scalable architecture for on-chip spectral discrimination, advancing CQD technology from single-band detection toward functional multispectral imaging.

As shown in Figure S28a, both the dark current and photocurrent in the NIR and SWIR bands exhibit a slight yet gradual degradation over time. We fully acknowledge that various configurations of CQDs-based dual-band detection have indeed been reported. However, it is critical to distinguish that all previous systems relied on mechanical pixel-by-pixel scanning–an approach inherently limited by low imaging speed, mechanically complexity, and impracticality for large-scale or real-time applications[1-3]. This fundamental constraint stemmed from the back-illuminated device architectures, fabricated on ITO-glass substrates (Figure 1), which are structurally and electrically incompatible with direct monolithic integration onto silicon ROICs.

The central advance of our work is therefore not merely another demonstration of dual-band detection, but the creation of a novel top-illuminated device architecture specifically engineered for monolithic integration into an FPA. This architectureal breakthrough overcomes a long-standing materials-processing integration challenge and was realized through several co-optimized innovations. Notably, we developed integration-aware band engineering that not only ensures compatibility with the ROIC fabrication process but also effectively suppresses dark current, thereby enabling high specific detectivity (>1011 cm·Hz1/2·W-1) across both the NIR and SWIR bands—performance that surpasses previously reported CQDs-based dual-color detectors.
Furthermore, we implemented active crosstalk suppression via a bias-tunable spectral response strategy, which minimizes inter-band interference and enables spectral discrimination during independent readout.
By combining this ROIC-compatible device architecture with a custom-designed readout system, we successfully demonstrate–for the first time–dual-band imaging using a monolithic CQDs FPA. This achievement marks a critical transition from single-pixel or scanned prototypes toward practical, scalable platform for multispectral imaging based on solution-processed quantum dot materials.

“Conventional dual-band NIR/SWIR imaging systems typically employ hybrid configurations of silicon (Si)-based NIR and indium gallium arsenide (InGaAs)-based SWIR detectors, requiring complex optical alignment and post-acquisition image fusion7. Although such systems achieve useful performance, their large footprint and high cost restrict deployment in resource-constrained or portable settings. Monolithic integration of dual-band photodetectors with readout integrated circuits (ROICs) on a single substrate represents a promising alternative, enabling substantial miniaturization and system-level cost reduction. Among integrated device architectures, vertically stacked photodiodes with back-to-back junction design allow bias-selectable spectral response while maintaining high pixel utilization—an essential feature for high-resolution dual-band imaging8.
Dual-band NIR and SWIR photodetectors based on back-to-back junction architectures have been demonstrated using a variety of material systems, including inorganic thin films (e.g., Si, Ge, GeSn)9,10, two-dimensional (2D) materials (e.g., MoS , black phosphorus)11,12, and colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) 2 (e.g., PbS, HgTe)13–15. However, Ge-based photodetectors suffer from relatively low detectivity in the SWIR range. Meanwhile, the practical deployment of 2D materials is hampered by the absence of scalable wafer-level synthesis and reliable heterointegration strategies, which limits their compatibility with FPAs manufacturing workflows9.
In contrast, CQDs, particularly those based on PbS, have emerged as a versatile material platform for both NIR and SWIR detection, owing to their bandgap tunability, solution processability, and inner compatibility with ROICs16. Vladimir et al. pioneered a vertically stacked n-p-n PbS CQDs photodiode architecture that enables bias-selectable dual-band detection across the NIR and SWIR regimes. Nevertheless, this device was implemented on a glass substrate using a back-illuminated configuration, rendering it incompatible with monolithic integration onto ROICs. Furthermore, CQDs-based dual-band photodetectors have so far been largely confined to single-pixel demonstrations, where performance is compromised by high dark current and non-negligible spectral crosstalk, there impeding their adoption in practical imaging application17.
Here, we report a top-illuminated, p-i-n-i-p structured dual-band photodetector based on two distinct sizes of PbS CQDs, enabling bias-switchable spectral response between the NIR and SWIR ranges. Through band engineering, the device achieves a specific detectivity exceeding 1×1011 cm·Hz1/2·W−1 in both bands, along with spectral crosstalk as low as 0.5%. By monolithically integrating the CQDs photodetector array with a custom-designed ROIC featuring bidirectional current sensing, we demonstrate a 128×128 dual-band infrared FPA capable of 57 NIR and SWIR imaging. This work establishes a scalable, Si-compatible route to high-performance dual-band infrared FPAs using solution-processed semiconductors.”
Comment 4-4:The manuscript does not clearly articulate the scientific challenge being addressed or the fundamental insight offered by this study. As a result, the broader implications for the CQD or imaging community remain unclear.
Response 4-4: We thank the reviewer for the opportunity to clarify the scientific significance of this work. In response, we have comprehensively restructured the manuscript to clearly define the fundamental challenge addressed and the conceptual advances offered by our study.
The core scientific challenge we tackle is the fundamental incompatibility between conventional CQDs device architectures—typically fabricated on ITO-glass substrates—and the structural requirements for direct monolithic integration with silicon-based ROICs. This mismatch has persistently hindered the transition of CQDs technology from single-pixel demonstrations to practical, scalable FPAs.
Our work provides three foundational insights that collectively address this challenge:
(1) A shift in device architecture: We present a top-illuminated dual-band CQDs photodetector architecture designed to enable monolithic integration with ROICs. This design addresses the inherent limitations of conventional back-illuminated devices fabricated on ITO/glass substrates, which are incompatible with front-side-coupled ROICs and thus hinder scalable FPA development. The proposed architecture provides a viable pathway toward integrated, large-format CQDs-based imaging systems.
(2) Investigation of band alignment: We elucidate the critical relationship between band alignment engineering and dark current suppression in vertically stacked CQDs heterojunctions, providing a design principle for managing charge transport in complex multi-junction devices.
(3) An operational strategy for spectral discrimination: We demonstrate a bias-tunable operational mode that actively mitigates inter-band crosstalk, thereby addressing a pervasive physical limitation in integrated CQDs dual-band photodetectors.
Collectively, these advances establish a scalable pathway for developing solution-processed, multi-spectral imaging systems. We have substantially revised the Introduction part to better highlight the scientific significance.

To more effectively demonstrate the spectral discrimination capability of our dual-band detector, we have redesigned several imaging scenes with enhanced color contrast, as shown in Figures 4d and 4e.
In Figure 4d, different inks exhibit distinct spectral behaviors: red ink is invisible in both NIR and SWIR; green ink is visible in NIR but attenuates in the SWIR; black ink remains clearly observable across both bands. These characteristics suggest potential utility in anti-counterfeiting applications. In Figure 4e, water and acetone in polyethylene bottles are indistinguishable under visible light. In FigureS37c, bruising on a plum is revealed in both NIR and SWIR; plums and pears show similar contrast in NIR, but differ clearly in SWIR due to skin reflectance differences.

Response 4-9: Thank the reviewer for such professional question.
The complete fabrication process of the PbS CQDs dual-band FPA is illustrated in Figure S30, with the detailed procedure described as follows. The process begins with cleaning the ROIC chip, followed by photolithography and electron-beam evaporation to deposit Ti/Au layers. These layers are patterned to extend the pixel-sized bottom electrodes to 12×12 μm. Two layers of solid-state ligand-exchanged PbS-EDT CQDs are then spin-coated onto the ROIC. Next, the SWIR PbS CQDs layer (PbS- II) is deposited via spin-coating of a solution containing liquid-phase ligand-exchanged PbS CQDs, followed by thermal drying. A 50 nm-thick C electron transport layer is then 60 deposited by thermal evaporation, followed by a 50 nm ZnO layer deposited via magnetron sputtering. Afterward, the NIR PbS CQDs layer (PbS-I) is spin-coated from a liquid-phase ligand-exchanged solution and thermally annealed to form a uniform film. Two additional layers of PbS-EDT are then spin-coated to serve as the hole transport layer. Finally, a 100 nm ITO transparent top electrode is deposited using sputtering. For device testing, the fabricated FPA chip is connected to a custom test board via wire bonding to access individual pixel signals.

Response 4-2: We thank the reviewer for this detailed observation. The apparent discrepancy arises from the difference in incident light intensity between the measurements. As shown in the linearity analysis in Figures S11 and S12, the photoresponse of the device is intensity-dependent. At low light intensities (< 0.01 W·cm−2), the responsivity at 1650 nm is essentially higher than that at 940 nm. Since photodetectors are primarily designed for weak signal detection, the EQE measurements (Panels 2d and 2e), which are performed under low-intensity monochromatic light, reflect the intrinsic, unsaturated performance of the device. At high light intensities (> 0.01 W·cm−2), The photocurrent in the 1650 nm band tends to saturate earlier than the 940 nm band. The data in Panels 2b/2c were acquired at higher intensities where this saturation occurs, making the 940 nm response appear relatively stronger.
Figure S11. LDRs of the dual-band photodetector measured under a bias of (a) +1 V with 940 nm illumination and (b) −1 V with 1650 nm illumination.
It is also important to note the relationship EQE = R×1240/λ (where R is responsivity). Even though the responsivity at 1650 nm is higher than at 940 nm in the linear regime, the larger denominator at 1650 nm reduces the calculated EQE value. Consequently, the peak EQE values for both bands appear comparable in Panels 2d/2e, despite the difference in responsivity. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have measured and included the full-wavelength EQE spectra (500–2000 nm) under both positive and negative biases. These results are now presented in Figure S13. They clearly show the bias-selectable spectral response across the entire range.
Regarding the suggestion for white-light EQE measurements, we respectfully note that standard EQE measurements utilizing monochromatic light are the established method for quantifying spectral cross-talk and specific detectivity. Configuring our setup for calibrated spectral extraction under broadband white-light illumination would require significant modification to the optical path. We believe the current monochromatic EQE data, combined with the crosstalk analysis provided, sufficiently characterizes the device’s spectral selectivity for realistic operating conditions.
